name: Household
plan: H6 unmarried: two co-adopters split $20,000 of adoption expenses 50/50 and each take the $5,000 refundable part of the adoption credit, section 23(a)(4)

tests.detail: The per-return $5,000 survives the strict reading, but with the section 23(c) carryforward valued the 50/50 plan is worse than one payer and the best split gains 0 to 574 nominal over the best one-payer filing.
Adding (a)(4) to section 23(i) leaves both baselines unmoved and removes the $5,000, but the adopt family still shows 1,951 from B's tax absorbing credit the default strands on A.
Without the adopt move the plan is gone; with only the adopt move it is found at 6,951; claim, keep, retirement and filing moves are decoration.
Without (a)(4) the $5,000 disappears but the search still returns 1,951 for the adopt family (payer choice under a model that drops the carryforward).
No conservation, limit, paid-amount, nonrefundable or refundable-cap violation in 39,706 plans and 11 stressed variants; two adults with no income get $10,000, which the text allows.

Plan, baselines, closed-gap result and six-year figures replay by decide; under the closed rule no move sequence from the default, for any facts, exceeds $5,000 refundable; axioms propext and Quot.sound only.
Python from the statute gives the same figures as the Lean, including the six-year ones.
No guidance divides the $5,000 between unmarried co-adopters and no writing found describes the plan; the IRS does read the $5,000 as per eligible child.

divergences: section 23(c) carryforward counted as lost (stated); the claimed figure depends on it
default has the adult with no tax left after section 24 pay all the expenses, adding 1,951 to the gain
adopt move offers only 0/50/100 percent; 50/50 strands 3,640 on A
section 23 amounts are 2025 ($5,000, $17,280) in a file labelled 2026 (reported 2026: $5,120, $17,670)
section 23(a)(2) year rule not modelled; expenses allowed in two years reach (a)(4) twice for any filer
sharing of the (b)(1) limit rests on Notice 97-9 and form instructions, not regulations; limit share tied to payment share where the instructions allow any agreed division
Facts.adoption, Plan.adoptA, Move.adopt, adoptShare and household H6 exist only for this plan
findings file attributes 'divide as they agree' to Notice 97-9; it is in the Form 8839 instructions

authority.quote: the $17,280 limit must be divided between the two of you. You can divide it in any way you both agree.

authority.source: Instructions for Form 8839 (2025), What's New and line 13
authority.quote: The amount of the refundable credit portion is determined separately for each eligible child.
an unmarried couple that seeks to adopt an eligible child must apply the $5,000 (or $6,000) limitation to the couple's combined qualified adoption expenses.
$5,000 of which may be refundable per child, if all other requirements are met.

authority.source: IRS adoption credit page (updated 19-Oct-2026); IR-2026-123 (16 Oct 2026)
authority.quote: For tax year 2025 only, unused adoption credit carryforwards from 2020–2024 may be refundable up to $5,000 per eligible child.
Any time a credit can produce a check from the government, fraudsters will pounce.

verdict_reason: Two unmarried co-adopters each get up to $5,000 refundable on the statute and the 2025 form, and no guidance divides it; but the $6,951 is 1,951 of baseline artifact plus 5,000 of acceleration, the lasting gain at these facts is 0 to 574 once the carryforward is valued, and the 50/50 split as found is 3,066 to 3,640 worse over six years than one adult paying everything.
